 Merck’s new South Korea facility highlights rising demand for advanced semiconductor chemicals 
 Merck has opened a new molybdenum production facility in South Korea to support next-generation chipmaking. The plant will make molybdenum dioxide dichloride, a key precursor for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, while also improving local supply and production reliability.Why this matters: If you follow the chip race, this is about more than one material. Merck is pairing its chemistry with delivery systems to help chipmakers build smaller, more complex devices with better efficiency, higher uptime and lower total cost.
Impact on Indian chemical sector: Merck’s new molybdenum facility supports demand for advanced chipmaking materials. For India’s chemical sector, the development highlights opportunities in specialty chemicals and semiconductor-grade materials, while increasing competition for technology, investment and supply capabilities as chipmakers seek more reliable materials for next-generation semiconductors.  Merck has opened a new molybdenum production facility in South Korea as chipmakers race to adapt to the demands of artificial intelligence and more complex device architectures. The investment is aimed at strengthening local supply, improving manufacturing reliability and widening the company’s role in advanced semiconductor materials, according to Indian Chemical News . The new site will make molybdenum dioxide dichloride, or MoO₂Cl₂, a precursor used in advanced chip production. The material will be paired with the company’s CHEMKEEPER delivery systems, creating an integrated package that combines chemistry and equipment for more efficient use of materials and steadier process performance. Why molybdenum is moving up the semiconductor agenda Molybdenum is gaining importance because the industry needs materials that can perform at smaller geometries and within increasingly complicated structures. Its use cases are expected to extend beyond three-dimensional NAND memory into DRAM wordlines and future logic devices, reflecting a wider shift in semiconductor design priorities. The precursor produced at the South Korean site is intended for chemical vapour deposition and atomic layer deposition, two processes central to making the thin films used in modern chips. When combined with the delivery systems, the setup is designed to support high-volume manufacturing with reliable material flow, high process uptime and material usage efficiency of more than 99 per cent, while also lowering overall ownership costs. AI is forcing a rethink of materials strategy The expansion comes at a time when artificial intelligence is accelerating the need for smaller, faster and more power-efficient chips. That shift is also pushing semiconductor suppliers to move beyond isolated material offerings and provide more integrated workflow solutions across the production chain. Benjamin Hein , Member of the Executive Board and CEO Electronics, said the industry can no longer rely on traditional scaling methods and isolated materials improvements alone. He said system integration would drive the next stage of innovation and described the molybdenum offering as an example of chemistry and delivery systems working together to support that shift. His remarks came during his first visit to South Korea since taking up the role on May 1, 2026, underscoring the strategic importance of the market for the company’s electronics business. Localising supply in Korea to serve regional chipmakers Bing Han , Executive Vice President and Head of the Thin Films Business Unit, said semiconductor customers are seeking new materials, dependable supply and faster time to market. He said molybdenum is becoming a critical material for smaller nodes and more intricate chip architectures. He added that the company has been localising its molybdenum solutions in South Korea through a supply chain that includes the new production site in Eumseong and delivery systems already being made at the Ansan site. That arrangement, he said, will strengthen supply security and help accelerate innovation for customers in South Korea and across Asia. The localisation push also reflects a broader industry trend. As geopolitical tensions, logistics disruptions and technology competition reshape semiconductor sourcing, chip manufacturers are increasingly favouring regional supply chains that can reduce lead times and cut dependence on distant production hubs. For materials suppliers, that means capacity is no longer enough on its own. Proximity, process integration and reliability are becoming equally important selling points. What the move means for the chip supply chain The South Korea facility gives the company a deeper foothold in one of Asia’s most important electronics ecosystems. It also signals how specialty chemical suppliers are positioning themselves not just as raw material vendors, but as partners in chip manufacturing performance. As the sector moves toward more advanced memory and logic technologies, demand is likely to rise for precursors that can deliver consistency at scale. The new plant is meant to address that need while reinforcing local production and helping customers improve throughput in a market where speed to innovation can determine competitiveness. For the broader semiconductor supply chain, the move highlights a simple reality: next-generation chips will depend as much on material science and delivery precision as on design breakthroughs. Suppliers that can combine both are likely to gain a stronger role in the race to support AI-era manufacturing.
